SDTM Module

Source: vignettes/sdtm-module.Rmd
sdtm-module.Rmd

Overview

This vignette shows how the aRtifacts core engine applies to SDTM (Study Data Tabulation Model) datasets. Everything here uses the same schema-agnostic snapshot/diff/rule machinery — the only thing that makes it “SDTM” is the data and the variable names you pass in.

Companion package roadmap: The SDTM-specific helpers demonstrated below are bundled in the core package today and will eventually move to a dedicated aRtifacts.sdtm companion package.

Step 1 — Load example LB data

example_sdtm_lb() returns a tiny synthetic Laboratory (LB) domain. In a real workflow you would read your production SDTM dataset instead.

library(aRtifacts)

lb <- example_sdtm_lb()
lb
#>   STUDYID DOMAIN     USUBJID LBSEQ LBTESTCD     LBTEST LBORRES LBORRESU
#> 1 STUDY01     LB STUDY01-001     1      HGB Hemoglobin    13.0     g/dL
#> 2 STUDY01     LB STUDY01-001     2      HGB Hemoglobin    13.4     g/dL
#> 3 STUDY01     LB STUDY01-002     1      HGB Hemoglobin    -1.0     g/dL
#> 4 STUDY01     LB STUDY01-002     2      HGB Hemoglobin    14.1     g/dL
#> 5 STUDY01     LB STUDY01-003     1      HGB Hemoglobin    15.0     g/dL
#>   LBSTRESN      LBDTC VISITNUM SITEID
#> 1     13.0 2024-01-01        1 SITE01
#> 2     13.4 2024-01-29        2 SITE01
#> 3     -1.0 2024-01-03        1 SITE01
#> 4     14.1 2024-01-31        2 SITE01
#> 5     15.0 2024-01-04        1 SITE02

Five records, three subjects, one test (Hemoglobin). Notice that subject STUDY01-002, sequence 1 has LBSTRESN = -1.0 — a negative lab value that we’ll catch below.

Step 2 — Snapshot and simulate a data refresh

Let’s create two snapshots representing successive data cuts. Between the cuts we’ll introduce realistic changes: a corrected value, a partial date, and a duplicate key row.

lb_old <- lb
lb_new <- lb

# Change 1: A numeric result becomes negative (data-entry error).
lb_new$LBSTRESN[lb_new$USUBJID == "STUDY01-002" & lb_new$LBSEQ == 2] <- -2.5

# Change 2: A full date is replaced with a partial date (formatting issue).
lb_new$LBDTC[lb_new$USUBJID == "STUDY01-003" & lb_new$LBSEQ == 1] <- "2024-01"

# Change 3: A new record arrives — but it duplicates an existing key.
lb_new <- rbind(lb_new, data.frame(
  STUDYID  = "STUDY01", DOMAIN = "LB",
  USUBJID  = "STUDY01-003", LBSEQ = 1,
  LBTESTCD = "HGB", LBTEST = "Hemoglobin",
  LBORRES  = "15.0", LBORRESU = "g/dL",
  LBSTRESN = 15.0,
  LBDTC    = "2024-01-04",
  VISITNUM = 1, SITEID = "SITE02",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
))

Now wrap each cut in a DomainSnapshot. The old cut is clean; the new one has the intentional problems.

snap_old <- new_domain_snapshot(
  name     = "LB",
  data     = lb_old,
  key_vars = c("STUDYID", "USUBJID", "LBSEQ")
)

Note: Creating a DomainSnapshot for lb_new will fail because the duplicate key (STUDY01-003 / LBSEQ 1) violates uniqueness. That’s the engine protecting you:

snap_new <- new_domain_snapshot(
  name     = "LB",
  data     = lb_new,
  key_vars = c("STUDYID", "USUBJID", "LBSEQ")
)
#> Error: <aRtifacts::DomainSnapshot> object is invalid:
#> - Rows are not unique by `key_vars`.

In practice you’d fix the source data. For demo purposes let’s remove the duplicate so we can continue:

lb_new <- lb_new[!duplicated(lb_new[, c("STUDYID", "USUBJID", "LBSEQ")]), ]

snap_new <- new_domain_snapshot(
  name     = "LB",
  data     = lb_new,
  key_vars = c("STUDYID", "USUBJID", "LBSEQ")
)

Step 3 — Diff the two snapshots

Key diff 

diff_keys(snap_old, snap_new)
#> $added
#> [1] STUDYID USUBJID LBSEQ  
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
#> 
#> $removed
#> [1] STUDYID USUBJID LBSEQ  
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

Both snapshots have the same key combinations — no records were added or removed. All changes are value-level.

Value diff 

diff_values(snap_old, snap_new, vars = c("LBSTRESN", "LBDTC"))
#>   STUDYID     USUBJID LBSEQ      var        old     new
#> 4 STUDY01 STUDY01-002     2 LBSTRESN       14.1    -2.5
#> 5 STUDY01 STUDY01-003     1    LBDTC 2024-01-04 2024-01

Two changes surface:

  • Subject 002, seq 2: LBSTRESN went from 14.1 → -2.5 (the injected error).
  • Subject 003, seq 1: LBDTC went from 2024-01-04 → 2024-01 (partial date).

These are exactly the edits we made — the diff engine picks them up deterministically with zero configuration.

Step 4 — Run generalized checks

check_tabulation_domain() applies structural and temporal checks from the core rule catalog. It works on any domain — here we point it at our modified LB dataset.

issues <- check_tabulation_domain(
  data              = lb_new,
  domain            = "LB",
  key_vars          = c("STUDYID", "USUBJID", "LBSEQ"),
  required_vars     = c("STUDYID", "USUBJID", "LBSEQ", "LBTESTCD", "LBDTC"),
  date_vars         = "LBDTC",
  non_negative_vars = "LBSTRESN",
  visit_order_var   = "VISITNUM",
  subject_var       = "USUBJID"
)

issues
#>                       check severity
#> 1          R013_DATE_FORMAT  warning
#> 2 R033_NEGATIVE_NOT_ALLOWED  warning
#>                                                                     message n
#> 1           LBDTC contains values that are not full ISO dates (YYYY-MM-DD). 1
#> 2 LBSTRESN contains negative values where non-negative values are expected. 2

Reading the output: Each row is one finding. The check column maps to a rule from the core catalog (e.g., R013_DATE_FORMAT, R033_NEGATIVE_NOT_ALLOWED). severity tells you whether it’s an error or warning. n tells you how many records are affected.

  • R013_DATE_FORMAT — LBDTC has a value that isn’t a full ISO date.
  • R033_NEGATIVE_NOT_ALLOWED — LBSTRESN contains a negative value where only non-negative values are expected.

Step 5 — Run rules as executable FlagRules

If you want row-level detail (not just summary counts), build an executable rule pack and run it through the flag engine.

art <- new_artifact_snapshot(domains = list(LB = snap_new), build_id = "cut-002")

rules <- make_rule_pack_core(
  domain            = "LB",
  key_vars          = c("STUDYID", "USUBJID", "LBSEQ"),
  required_vars     = c("STUDYID", "USUBJID", "LBSEQ", "LBTESTCD", "LBDTC"),
  non_negative_vars = "LBSTRESN"
)

flags <- run_flags(art, rules)
flags
#>   STUDYID     USUBJID LBSEQ SITEID LBSTRESN VARIABLE VALUE
#> 3 STUDY01 STUDY01-002     1 SITE01     -1.0 LBSTRESN  -1.0
#> 4 STUDY01 STUDY01-002     2 SITE01     -2.5 LBSTRESN  -2.5
#>                     RULE_ID DOMAIN SEVERITY   CATEGORY OWNER_TEAM
#> 3 R033_NEGATIVE_NOT_ALLOWED     LB  warning data_entry   Biostats
#> 4 R033_NEGATIVE_NOT_ALLOWED     LB  warning data_entry   Biostats

Each flagged row is returned with the RULE_ID, SEVERITY, and OWNER_TEAM that produced it. You can filter, sort, or export this table into any downstream reporting pipeline.
